sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
sources.text: As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’ Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead. The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back. “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return.” The comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that in turn are supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries. Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang. The reinstatement letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. The former Nvidia CEO resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who is no relation. His resignation ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded. Days earlier, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife without specifying who else was involved. Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that [Alice Huang] is a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in his administration. According to the Financial Times , Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for his return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. The FT also reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang. One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Colette Kress , Nvidia’s chief financial officer – the best option. “We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”. The new rule announced by the US government on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted. “The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Department of Commerce said. Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, worked as an executive at the Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. According to reports, Megaspeed is under suspicion of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws. Megaspeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complied “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”. Nvidia shares closed down 4.1% on Monday, knocking about $160bn (£121bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.76tn compared with $4.5tn before the scandal broke.

sources.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
sources.text: Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless. This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next? Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. With the rise of personal AI assistants, the internet isn't just for humans anymore. sources.title: Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, source tells CNBC
sources.text: Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets. Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia. Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies. Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that Huang had not discussed a comeback with him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on speculation on Sunday. Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has drawn 180,000 signatures as well as support from major figures including Elon Musk , Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Jensen Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia. "It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. On Friday, a representative for Nvidia's board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role.

Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, according to a report from CNBC . A source tells the outlet the board “is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back.” Since Huang’s resignation last week , tech executives, along with current and former Nvidia employees, have called for his reinstatement. An online petition to bring Huang back as CEO has amassed more than 180,000 signatures , including from major figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad. A report from the Financial Times also suggests that Huang floated the idea of returning as CEO with some of his colleagues. Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The company has also hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang’s conduct .

sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: Nvidia's board reportedly won't consider reinstating Jensen Huang
sources.text: Petition to bring back Huang is now closing in on 200,000 signatures Following the resignation of Jensen Huang , there's been a campaign to reinstate Nvidia's recently departed CEO — but reports suggest that the company's board does not intend to do so. The Financial Times claims that Nvidia 's board is "not considering reinstating Jensen Huang" as CEO, according to anonymous sources with inside knowledge of the situation. We were told in a previous report from the FT that Huang is mulling a potential return, perhaps buoyed by the open letter signed by his supporters, which now has over 190,000 signatures. As well as Elon Musk, who is the most prominent name among the high-profile signatories from the tech world, Huang apparently now has the support of US President Donald Trump. The FT quotes Trump as saying: "I think having Jensen go back … that certainly isn't a bad idea." That's not exactly a wholehearted recommendation, granted, but the gist is clear enough. Trump also noted that the Chinese spy accusations around the woman who Huang had an affair with remain unproven. In a further show of support for Huang, Central News Agency reports that the Taipei 101 skyscraper (the tallest building in Taiwan) displayed a lit billboard (see the video clip below) with messages aiming to "win back" Huang, including one that simply read "Taiwan ♡ Jensen". This was funded by some key players in Taiwan's tech industry, including the Taipei Computer Association and Taipei Components Association. Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. With the bring back Huang petition now reaching close to 200,000 signatures (doubtless it'll get there later today), and various displays of support for the ex-CEO (quite literal displays in the case of Taipei), you'd be forgiven for thinking that maybe he does have a chance of making a comeback. I said that was unlikely yesterday, though, and this new FT report appears to back up that notion in no uncertain terms. This just isn't something the board can consider; at least not based on some generalized shows of support and a petition, anyway. Nvidia's board has moved on, and is now working on the search for a successor. Approaches have already been made, with the FT informing us that one of the potential candidates Team Green has been in touch with is Rene Haas, the current CEO of Arm . On the face of it, Haas seems like a strong candidate for the role (and he was previously VP of computing products at Nvidia, albeit some time ago, having left in 2013). Whether he could be persuaded to jump ship from Arm, though, is unclear. The problem is that taking the reins from Huang is more than a tall order, with the upper structure of Nvidia's top execs very much built around the ex-CEO (Huang seemingly had some 50 or more direct reports, which is a huge number for a chief exec to manage). This is why there's also talk of perhaps splitting the role into co-CEOs, and that tactic could fly with internal appointments. One theory ( as per Business Insider ) is that Colette Kress (the CFO and current interim chief exec) and Ian Buck (VP of Hyperscale and HPC Computing) could share the job, taking control over the financial side and product direction respectively. That could be a longer-term semi-permanent co-CEO solution, as it were, while a true successor is worked out. This uncertainty, and the perceived difficulty of replacing Huang, is why there's suddenly a big cloud of doubt over Nvidia's future. While revenue over the next year (or even longer) is nailed down, what happens beyond that is where the situation gets a lot less clear, and the board is doubtless feeling quite some pressure to be seen as being on top of finding a solution. sources.text: Amante espiã: entenda o que levou à renúncia do CEO da Nvidia Fofoca envolvendo traição, espionagem e as duas maiores superpotências do mundo é prato cheio para o 'Guia Do Adulto Premium'. Crédito: Roteiro e Apresentação: Larissa Burchard / Produção: Sara Helen / Edição de Vídeo: Felipe Pahor O conselho de diretores da Nvidia não está considerando oficialmente recolocar Jensen Huang no cargo de CEO . A informação não é oficial, mas teria sido confirmada por fontes ligadas à empresa a veículos como CNBC e The Wall Street Journal . Especulações sobre uma possível tentativa de Huang de voltar à empresa após a renúncia na última quinta-feira (12) circularam e citavam uma vontade do próprio executivo , além de uma pressão exercida por apoiadores para restituir o antigo gerente à posição. Ao mesmo tempo, a companhia já teria iniciado a busca por uma pessoa para substituir o cofundador da empresa, que ficou mais de três décadas no cargo. Enquanto o cargo é ocupado interinamente por Colette Kress, atual vice-presidente executiva e diretora financeira, o CEO da rival Arm teria sido consultado sobre uma possível contratação. De acordo com as fontes, que permaneceram anônimas devido ao sigilo da situação, o conselho da Nvidia está totalmente focado em seguir com as investigações envolvendo os relacionamentos extraconjugais do CEO. O primeiro dos casos revelados é o que mais pesa contra o retorno do empresário: Alice Huang é acusada de ser uma espiã chinesa, além de estar diretamente envolvida na negociação de chips da Nvidia inclusive com empresas do país asiático. Oficialmente, Huang não se manifestou sobre o caso, mas teria ficado abatido com as revelações concordou em prestar um depoimento ao Congresso dos Estados Unidos para explicar a relação com Alice e os possíveis conflitos de interesse envolvendo a política externa do país. stories.summary: Nvidia's stock continued to slide on Monday following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Nvidia stock falls as investors price in fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation
sources.text: Nvidia 's stock slid 4.12% Monday in the wake of CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation , leading a broader chipmaker selloff after the chip giant lost hundreds of billions in market cap last week. The continued decline since Huang's resignation brought Nvidia's stock to its lowest close since July 1, 2025. Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, after mounting scrutiny following reports that he had a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. It was later reported that Huang had romantic relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday. An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 170,000 signatures , as prominent tech executives, including Elon Musk , rallied behind him. A source familiar with the matter told CNBC, however, that Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Huang. Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers are pushing to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company through its meteoric rise to becoming the world's most valuable company, with its AI chips underpinning the technology's boom. Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia, adding that the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls. — CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
sources.text: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most. But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great. “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says. Already, competitors have started to move in. Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026. Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia. Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models. Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025. And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes. Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups. In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale. While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms. Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere. Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says. Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips. Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch. Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes. But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
sources.text: CEO ousted after affair with suspected Chinese spy reportedly plans comeback, but US treasury secretary urges ‘dramatic shake-up’ Megaspeed says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’ Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation. An open letter that has more than 165,000 signatories demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded, after reports he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate. According to the Financial Times , Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌CEO’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support. On Friday, two big shareholders, the investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open. In Washington, however, the US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look outside the company for its next CEO. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News. Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it had knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing, Alice Huang. The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence. In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to China, but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society. “Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”. Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days. One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress – the best option. “We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”. US lawmakers have said Donald Trump’s administration must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy. Jensen Huang has agreed to appear before the House select committee on China, as well as the foreign affairs and the intelligence committees. The dates of the appearances, likely to be behind closed doors, have not been confirmed. On Sunday, Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company where Alice Haung was an executive until she left in 2025, said it was a “ legitimate and lawful business ”. In the past three years, the company was one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, buying nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) in AI chips and advanced hardware. Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Jensen Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, the founder and CEO of the video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, the president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator. Another signatory, the Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”. More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce. The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen within the industry as a godfather of AI . Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”. But the company – which will report on its quarterly earnings on Tuesday – has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with the Claude creator, Anthropic, and its chief executive, Dario Amodei. sources.text: Por André Lourenti Magalhães • Editado por Jones Oliveira | 16/11/2026 às 14:02 Jensen Huang renunciou ao cargo de CEO da NVIDIA na última semana, mas não descarta voltar ao comando da empresa. De acordo com o site Financial Times, Huang conta com aliados no Vale do Silício para pressionar o conselho da Big Tech sobre um possível retorno . Uma das fontes ouvidas pela reportagem original afirma que há uma “sala de guerra” montada por parceiros e lobistas para trazê-lo de volta ao cargo. Há até a possibilidade de buscar apoio na Casa Branca, ainda que o caminho seja improvável — o Secretário do Tesouro dos EUA, Scott Bessent, já defendeu publicamente uma reestruturação na empresa de chips. Um dos argumentos dos aliados é de que Jensen Huang é uma pessoa querida no mercado de tecnologia. Outras fontes afirmam que o ex-CEO era o responsável por conduzir negociações importantes no mercado de IA. Um eventual retorno é apoiado até por funcionários da própria NVIDIA : comentários em caixa de sugestões internas da companhia defendem a volta do executivo. Por enquanto, a companhia é liderada de forma interina por Colette Kress, que atuava como vice-presidente executiva e diretora financeira antes da mudança. Jensen Huang também é defendido por nomes importantes do mercado, como Elon Musk e o CEO da Epic Games, Tim Sweeney . Ambos assinaram uma carta aberta pedindo para o conselho “trazer Jensen de volta” . A NVIDIA ainda não tem novas atualizações sobre o comando da empresa, mas rumores apontam que o CEO da Arm, Rene Haas, seria um dos favoritos a assumir a cadeira deixada por Huang. Jensen Huang renunciou ao cargo após confirmar um caso extraconjugal com a ex-diretora da Megaspeed International e empresária Alice Huang, acusada de espionagem a favor da China.
